questions.q: Customers forward receipts to employers, who must be able to check that a receipt really came from your shop. Employers will never hold any secret of yours. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: The need is public verifiability: anyone can check, only you can create. A signature separates the two abilities. HMAC needs the shared secret to check, and a plain hash has no key, so anyone could compute one for an edited receipt.
options: HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret
AES-256-GCM encryption
A digital signature (for example Ed25519) with a published public key
A SHA-256 hash printed on the receipt

questions.q: Why is HMAC a poor choice when many outside parties must verify your messages?
questions.explain: HMAC is symmetric: one key both creates and checks. That is fine between parties that trust each other (your own services, a payment provider and you), but not when verifiers must not be able to forge.
options: HMAC is slower than signatures
HMAC tags are too long to send
Checking an HMAC needs the same secret that creates it, so every verifier could also create valid messages
HMAC only works on text, not bytes

questions.q: A mobile app caches the product catalogue on the phone and wants to notice if the file got corrupted on disk. What is enough?
questions.explain: The threat is an accident, not an attacker, so integrity without a key is enough. Choose the smallest tool that gives the promise you need; a signature would add key management for no benefit here.
options: A SHA-256 checksum stored with the file
An Ed25519 signature
AES-256-GCM encryption
scrypt

questions.q: You store customers' dates of birth and must show them on the profile page. What should protect them at rest?
questions.explain: You must read the value back, so it needs encryption, not hashing. Base64 is encoding: anyone can decode it. A signature proves authenticity but hides nothing.
options: SHA-256, because hashes cannot be reversed
Base64, so they are not readable at a glance
Authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM) with a key from a secret store
An Ed25519 signature

questions.q: With Ed25519, which key creates signatures and which checks them?
questions.explain: Only the holder of the private key can sign. The public key can be published and used by anyone to verify; node:crypto even refuses to sign with a public key object.
options: The public key signs, the private key verifies
The private key signs, the public key verifies
Both sides use the same key for both
Either key can do either job

questions.q: Two parties run an X25519 key exchange over the internet. What does the key exchange alone not give them?
questions.explain: A key exchange defeats passive eavesdroppers, but it does not authenticate the public keys. An active man-in-the-middle can run one exchange with each side. TLS adds certificates and a signature over the handshake to close that gap.
options: A shared secret that an eavesdropper cannot compute
Proof of who is on the other end, so someone in the middle could swap the public keys
A key that can be turned into an AES key
Protection against someone who only listens

questions.q: Why does the lesson pass the key-exchange result through HKDF with a label such as "shop session v1"?
questions.explain: A raw key-exchange output should not be used directly as a key. HKDF derives uniform keys and binds each to a purpose, so one shared secret can safely produce separate keys for separate jobs.
options: To make the shared secret shorter
To encrypt the shared secret
To turn it into a proper key for one specific purpose; a different label gives an unrelated key
Because diffieHellman returns text

questions.q: TLS uses asymmetric cryptography during the handshake, then switches to AES-GCM or ChaCha20 for the data. Why not use asymmetric cryptography for everything?
questions.explain: This combination is hybrid encryption: each kind of cryptography does the job it is good at.
options: Asymmetric algorithms cannot handle binary data
Asymmetric operations are much slower; they are used to agree on keys and prove identity, then fast symmetric encryption protects the data
Symmetric encryption is more secure in every way
Browsers do not support asymmetric encryption

questions.q: Which of these does TLS not promise?
questions.explain: TLS protects data in transit and authenticates the server. What the server does with the data afterwards is up to its own security: encryption at rest, access control, and so on.
options: Nobody on the café Wi-Fi can read the request
Nobody can change the response in transit without it being detected
The server really is the host named in the certificate
The server will store your card number safely after it arrives

questions.q: A client connects to api.shop.example and receives a valid, CA-signed certificate for blog.example. What must it do?
questions.explain: A certificate proves that a key belongs to a name. A genuine certificate for another name proves nothing about this host; anyone can get a valid certificate for a domain they own.
options: Accept it, because a trusted CA signed it
Accept it but log a warning
Refuse the connection, because the certificate does not name the host it wanted
Retry with plain HTTP

questions.q: In development, a request to your local HTTPS server fails with DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT. What is the right fix?
questions.explain: The first two accept any certificate from anyone, which removes server authentication, and they tend to leak into production. Trusting exactly your development certificate keeps every check on.
options: Set rejectUnauthorized: false on the request
Set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 in the shell
Trust that specific certificate or your local development CA (the ca option, or NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS)
Switch the server to HTTP

questions.q: What does "self-signed certificate" mean?
questions.explain: Issuer and subject are the same. Nothing outside vouches for it, so clients reject it unless they have been told to trust that exact certificate.
options: A certificate that has no signature
A certificate signed by its own private key rather than by a certificate authority
A certificate that the browser signs when it first sees it
A certificate with an expired signature

questions.q: A production API key was committed and pushed to a public repository an hour ago. What comes first?
questions.explain: Scanners find public keys within minutes, and clones already contain it. Only revoking makes the copy useless. Then investigate how it was used, then clean the history.
options: Rewrite the Git history to remove the commit
Make the repository private
Revoke the key and switch to a new one, so the leaked one stops working
Add the file to .gitignore

questions.q: Your secrets are injected as environment variables. What does a secret store (such as Vault or a cloud secret manager) add?
questions.explain: Environment variables are a delivery mechanism, visible to the whole process and often to crash reports. The store is where secrets are managed: who may read which one, who did, and which version is current.
options: Nothing: environment variables are already encrypted
Access control per service, an audit log of reads, and versioned secrets that make rotation practical
Faster startup
It lets you commit secrets to Git safely

questions.q: Which services should hold the private key that signs receipts?
questions.explain: Least privilege: each service gets only the secrets it uses. Verifying needs only the public key, which is not secret.
options: Every service, so any of them can sign if one is down
The web front end, because it shows receipts
Only the receipts service (or better, a KMS it calls), while everyone else gets the public key
The database, next to the receipts

questions.q: A colleague wants to reuse the payment webhook HMAC secret to sign session cookies too, "to have fewer secrets". What is the problem?
questions.explain: Keep one key per purpose. If both must come from one master secret, derive separate keys with HKDF and different labels.
options: There is no problem; HMAC is HMAC
One key, two purposes: a value valid for one could be accepted by the other, and rotating or leaking one affects both
Cookies cannot be signed with HMAC
Webhook secrets are too short for cookies

questions.q: What is the right order for rotating a signing key without breaking verification?
questions.explain: Verifiers must know the new public key before they see signatures made with it, and old signatures must keep verifying until they no longer matter.
options: Delete the old key, create the new key, start signing
Start signing with the new key, then publish its public key
Add and publish the new key, switch signing to it, retire the old key when nothing needs it
Retire the old key, wait a week, add the new key

questions.q: A signed token carries kid: "receipts-2026-09". How should the verifier use it?
questions.explain: The key id only selects among keys the verifier already trusts. Letting the message supply the key or the algorithm hands the decision to whoever wrote the message.
options: Download the key from a URL given in the token
Use whatever algorithm the token's header names
Look the id up in its own set of trusted keys, and refuse the token if the id is unknown
Ignore it and try every key it has until one works

questions.q: Why should a verifier check the signature on the exact received bytes, before calling JSON.parse?
questions.explain: Verify, then parse, then act. Genuine messages keep verifying, and forged ones never reach code that trusts their content.
options: Because JSON.parse is slow
Signatures cover bytes; re-serialised JSON can differ in spacing or key order, and unverified input should not reach the parser at all
Because signatures only work on base64
It does not matter which comes first

questions.q: What does a KMS or HSM give you that a key stored in an environment variable does not?
questions.explain: If your server is compromised, an attacker can use the KMS while they have access, but cannot copy the key and keep using it afterwards. That limits the damage to the time of the breach.
options: Faster signatures
The private key never leaves the KMS; your service asks it to sign or decrypt, and every use can be logged
Automatic HTTPS
Protection against bugs in your authorization code

questions.q: In envelope encryption, what does the KMS encrypt?
questions.explain: Encrypting large data locally is fast, and the KMS only handles small keys. A leaked database is useless without access to the KMS to unwrap the data keys.
options: Every database record, one by one
Only the small data keys; the records themselves are encrypted locally with those data keys
Nothing; it only stores the keys in plain text
The TLS traffic

questions.q: Ed25519 signatures are deterministic: the same key and message always give the same signature. Why is that an advantage?
questions.explain: A reused or predictable nonce in ECDSA can reveal the private key. Ed25519 derives its nonce from the key and message, removing that failure mode. Deterministic does not mean forgeable: you still need the private key.
options: It makes signatures shorter
There is no per-signature random nonce that an implementation could get wrong, a mistake that has leaked private keys in older ECDSA code
It lets anyone recompute the signature without the key
It makes signatures secret

questions.q: What does exporting a public key as a JWK print?
questions.explain: Ed25519 keys use key type OKP. A public JWK has only x, the 32-byte public key; the private part d is never in it, which is what makes it safe to publish.
options: OKP Ed25519 false 32
OKP Ed25519 true 32
EC Ed25519 false 64
RSA Ed25519 false 32

questions.explain: During the overlap both keys verify; after retiring k1, tokens signed with it are refused. An unknown id is always refused. In real code the check would also verify the signature with the key the id selects.

ok (k1) ok (k2)

questions.q: What does util.parseEnv give for this .env text?
questions.explain: Comments are skipped and quotes around values are removed. The empty placeholder becomes an empty string, not a missing key, so a startup check must treat "" as invalid, not just undefined.
options:
{ PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET: '', SHOP_NAME: 'Mama Put Stores' }
true 2

{ SHOP_NAME: 'Mama Put Stores' }

questions.q: Write chooseTool(need) that maps a need to a tool name. need has boolean fields password, readBack, outsidersVerify, sharedSecretOk. Rules, in order: a password needs "scrypt"; data you read back needs "aes-256-gcm"; outsiders verifying needs "ed25519"; parties sharing a secret need "hmac-sha256"; otherwise "sha256".
questions.explain: The order encodes the reasoning: a password is never encrypted or signed, only slow-hashed; anything you must read back needs encryption; anything strangers verify needs a signature; a shared secret between trusted parties allows HMAC; and a plain hash is only for accidents.
questions.expected:
user login -> scrypt
seller bank account -> aes-256-gcm
receipts for employers -> ed25519
warehouse stock updates -> hmac-sha256
catalogue checksum -> sha256

questions.q: Write certCovers(names, host): names is the list of DNS names in a certificate. Return true if any name matches the host exactly (ignoring case), or is a wildcard *.rest where the host has exactly one extra label in front of rest.
questions.explain: Matching the suffix .shop.example (with its leading dot) prevents evilshop.example from matching, and requiring no further dot in the prefix limits the wildcard to one label. Real TLS libraries do this for you; the point is to know what a wildcard certificate does and does not cover.
questions.expected:
shop.example true
API.shop.example true
a.b.shop.example false
shop.example.net false
evilshop.example false

questions.q: Write keyFor(keys, kid). keys is an object from key id to { status }, where status is "active", "verify-only" or "retired". Return the key if it may be used to verify (active or verify-only), otherwise null. Ids that are not own properties of keys (such as "toString") must return null.
questions.explain: keys["toString"] would find the function inherited from Object.prototype; Object.hasOwn refuses it. Listing which statuses are allowed (instead of which are refused) keeps a new status such as "compromised" refused by default.
questions.expected:
receipts-2026-09 active
receipts-2026-06 verify-only
receipts-2026-03 null
receipts-1999 null
toString null

questions.q: Write signingKid(keys) that returns the id of the single key whose status is "active". If there is no active key, or more than one, throw an Error with the message "expected exactly one active key, found N".
questions.explain: A half-finished rotation (no active key, or two) is a configuration error. Failing loudly at startup is much better than signing with whichever key happens to come first.
questions.expected:
k2
expected exactly one active key, found 0
expected exactly one active key, found 2

questions.q: Write badSecrets(env, names) that returns the names (in the given order) whose value is missing, empty, shorter than 32 characters, or one of the placeholders "changeme" or "TODO". Never include the values in the result.
questions.explain: Placeholders copied from an example file are a real deployment mistake; a length check alone would have let a long placeholder through, so check both. Returning names only means the result can be logged safely.

questions.q: Write expiringSoon(certs, now, days) that returns the hosts of certificates whose notAfter (milliseconds) is less than days days after now, including already expired ones, sorted by notAfter, soonest first.
questions.explain: An expired certificate is the most urgent, so it sorts first. A daily job like this, alerting well before expiry, is the safety net behind automatic renewal.

questions.q: Signed messages carry { purpose, issuer, expiresAt, data } inside the signed bytes. The signature has already been verified. Write acceptFor(expected, message, now) that returns message.data only if purpose and issuer match expected and now is before expiresAt; otherwise return a string saying which check failed first ("purpose", "issuer" or "expired").
questions.explain: A valid signature only says who signed. These checks make sure the message is being used for what it was signed for, by the expected signer, and while it is still valid: the same job the aud, iss and exp claims do in a JWT. Writing !(now < expiresAt) also refuses a missing or non-numeric expiry.
